title: TRUE and FALSE: what a comparison returns

screens.prompt: In B9, answer TRUE when the total units are over 100.

hints.syntax: =SUM(B2:B7)>100: add the units first, then compare the result.
hints.func-sum: The question is about the total, so the six units have to be added inside the formula.
hints.require-ref: Add the cells in B2:B7 rather than typing 150.
hints.value: The items come to 150, and 150 is over 100, so the cell should show TRUE.
hints.error: A division inside the comparison leaves #DIV/0!, and the cell shows that instead of TRUE or FALSE.

reject.why: the words TRUE and FALSE are text, not the logical values
the comparison points the wrong way, so it answers FALSE
typing the answer as text never adds anything up
the range starts on row 3, so the first item is left out of the total
division by zero, so the cell holds #DIV/0!
the range sits outside the parentheses

screens.prompt: In B9, answer TRUE when the average units are at least 20.

hints.syntax: =AVERAGE(B2:B7)>=20: the comparison takes the whole average as its left side.
hints.func-average: The question asks about the average, so a total of 150 would answer a different one.
hints.require-ref: Average the units column of the grid.
hints.value: 150 across six items is 25 each, which clears 20, so the answer is TRUE.
hints.error: Here #DIV/0! comes from dividing by zero in the comparison, not from AVERAGE over a full range.

reject.why: the total is 150 and would pass almost any threshold, which is not the question
the average is 25, so a stricter threshold answers FALSE
the range starts on row 3, so the first item is left out of the average
division by zero, so the cell holds #DIV/0!
the words TRUE and FALSE are text, not the logical values
the range sits outside the parentheses

docs.syntax: =SUM(B2:B7)>100 returns TRUE or FALSE; it is the comparison, not a word
docs.explain:
A comparison is a formula in its own right. Enter =SUM(B2:B7)>100 and the cell holds TRUE, a logical value that IF, AND and conditional formatting all read directly. Wrap the word in quotes and the cell holds four characters of text, which sorts with labels and fails a logical test.

The six items add to 150, so the first screen answers TRUE. The second screen asks about the average, which is 25 units and clears a floor of 20. Point the operator the other way and the same numbers answer FALSE.

An IF wrapped around a comparison only passes along a value that was already worked out. Put the comparison in quotes instead, as in =IF(SUM(B2:B7)>100,"TRUE","FALSE"), and the cell returns two pieces of text that nothing else can test.

errors.text: The cell holds the four characters TRUE as text, so a later IF reads a label where it expected a logical value.
A function name or a cell reference was mistyped, so Excel cannot tell which cells to compare.
The comparison is divided by zero, so the cell shows an error where TRUE or FALSE belonged.

docs.atWork: Flagging a month as over budget, then letting the next formula act on the flag.
docs.outcome: Read a comparison as a logical value that other formulas can act on.
docs.teaches: comparison operators returning logical values, and why quoted TRUE is not one
docs.dataset: Stock list with a total row to compare against

seo.title: TRUE and FALSE in Excel: logical values
seo.description: A comparison hands back a logical value, not the word TRUE. Type the word in quotes and IF will not take it, and a sort files it with your text.
